section.title: Improper integrals
section.p: The last section ended with a warning. A definite integral over a closed, finite interval is safe when the integrand is continuous. The interval has finite length, the function stays bounded, and the accumulated amount is a finite number.
But many natural accumulations do not fit that safe pattern.

A radioactive particle may decay forever. A probability density may stretch over the whole real line. A force law may blow up near a point. A curve may enclose an infinite region whose area is still finite.
So we have to ask a more careful question:
section.md: \text{When does an infinite or singular accumulation have a finite value?}
section.p: That is the question of improper integrals.
An improper integral is not wrong or badly formed. The word improper means that the integral lies outside the original definition and must be interpreted as a limit.

subsection.title: Convergence and divergence
subsection.p: The words convergent and divergent describe the limiting process, not the antiderivative.
An improper integral converges if the limiting accumulated amount approaches a finite number. It diverges if the limiting accumulated amount does not approach a finite number.
The antiderivative may exist on every finite subinterval and the improper integral may still diverge.

exercise.title: Why can an antiderivative exist on every finite piece while the improper integral diverges?

statement.p: For every finite t>1, \int_1^t(1/x)\,dx=\ln t exists, but \int_1^\infty(1/x)\,dx diverges. In your own words, why do the words convergent and divergent describe the limiting accumulated amount, not the existence of an antiderivative?

hint.p: Convergence means the running total approaches a finite number. An antiderivative on each compact subinterval is not the same as a finite total for the whole improper accumulation.

exercise.title: Why can comparison decide convergence without finding a value?

statement.p: The integral \int_1^\infty e^{-x^2}\,dx has no elementary antiderivative, yet it converges because e^{-x^2}\le e^{-x} for x\ge1. In your own words, why is a smaller nonnegative area finite when a larger comparison area is finite, and why are the p-integrals a useful comparison family?

hint.p: If you already know a larger nonnegative tail has finite area, a smaller tail cannot have infinite area. The power 1/x^p is a catalog of tails whose convergence is settled, so you can match an unknown tail to a known one.

Improper integrals teach a useful discipline. Do not evaluate first and ask questions later. First ask where the integral is improper. Then replace the dangerous endpoint or discontinuity by a limit. Then decide whether the limit is finite.
The next section collects the mistakes this discipline prevents.
